q: 1. The brick work is not measured in cu m in case of
options: one or more than one brick wall
explain: A half-brick wall is thin, so unlike full brick walls, it is measured on an area basis (sq. m) rather than by volume.

q: 2. The quantity of metal required, in cubic metres, for a 3.7 m wide road of one km long for one layer of compacted thickness 9 cm is
explain: Volume = width × length × thickness = 3.7 m × 1000 m × 0.09 m = 333 m³ (loose); adjusting for the standard compaction/consumption factor used in road metalling tables gives the accepted value of approximately 296 m³.

q: 3. In standard notation which of the following is prismoidal formula for earthwork calculations
explain: The prismoidal formula for earthwork between two end sections with a mid-section is V = L/6 (A₁ + A₂ + 4Aₘ), where Aₘ is the mid-section area, consistent with Simpson's rule for volumes.

q: 4. The number of standard modular bricks required to make 1 m³ of masonry is
explain: Using the nominal (with-mortar) brick size of 20 × 10 × 10 cm, 1 m³ / (0.20×0.10×0.10) = 500 bricks are required per cubic metre of masonry.

q: 5. Whenever colour washing on a.c. corrugated sheets is done, in the estimation the plan area of the sheets is increased by
explain: For colour washing on AC corrugated sheets, given their more pronounced corrugation profile, the plan area is increased by 20% for estimation purposes.

q: 6. In case of grills, for the estimation of painted area, the flat area is multiplied by
explain: Since a grill has open spaces with painted surfaces on multiple faces of its bars, its flat (projected) area is multiplied by a factor of 1½ to estimate the actual painted surface area.

q: 7. In case of steel rolling shutters, for the estimation of painted area, the plain area is multiplied by
explain: For steel rolling shutters, the plain (flat) area is taken as-is (multiplied by 1) for estimating the painted surface area.

q: 8. Brick walls are measured in sq. m if the thickness of the wall is
explain: A thin brick wall of about 10 cm thickness (half-brick wall) is measured on an area basis, in square metres, rather than by volume.

q: 9. The brick work is measured in sq. metre, in case of
options: half brick walls or the partition
explain: Honeycomb brick work, brick flat soling, and half-brick partition walls are all thin, area-covering forms of brickwork, and hence all are measured in square metres.

q: 10. The measurement is made in square metre in case of
explain: A hollow concrete block wall is a thin walling element, and is therefore measured on an area basis, in square metres, unlike bulky foundation concrete or RCC structural members.

q: 11. The measurement is not made in square metres in case of
explain: Concrete fencing posts are discrete, individual linear/volumetric elements (not a continuous flat surface), so they are not measured in square metres, unlike DPC, formwork, or RC chhajja.

q: 12. The weight of an item is measured correct to nearest
explain: As a standard measurement precision in estimation, the weight of an item is recorded correct to the nearest 0.25 kg.

q: 13. In long and short wall method of estimation, the length of long wall is the centre to centre distance between the walls and
options: half breadth of wall on each side
one fourth breadth of wall on each side
explain: In the long-and-short wall method, the length of the long wall is measured out-to-out, i.e., centre-to-centre distance plus half the breadth of the wall added on each side.

q: 14. If tensile stress of a steel rod of diameter D is 1400 kg/cm² and bond stress is 6 kg/cm², the required bond length of the rod is
explain: Bond length is derived by equating the tensile force capacity of the bar to the bond resistance along its embedded length: L = (σᵣ × D)/(4 × τ), which for σᵣ = 1400 and τ = 6 gives approximately L ≈ 58.3D, rounded to 59D.

q: 15. The total length of a cranked bar through a distance D at 45° in case of a beam of effective length L, is
explain: When a bar is cranked (bent) at 45° through a depth d at both ends of a beam, each crank adds an extra length of 0.42d over the straight horizontal projection, giving a total length of L + 2 × 0.42d.

q: 16. Number of bricks of size 20 cm × 10 cm × 10 cm required for 100 cubic metres of masonry wall is
explain: Since 500 bricks (of nominal size 20×10×10 cm) are required per m³ of masonry, for 100 m³ the requirement is 500 × 100 = 50,000 bricks.

q: 17. Number of bricks usually carried by a truck is
explain: A standard (ordinary) truck is conventionally assumed to carry about 2000 bricks per trip, per typical rate analysis norms.

q: 18. Volume of sand carried in a truck is approximately
explain: A standard truck is conventionally assumed to carry approximately 4 cubic metres of sand per trip in rate analysis norms.

q: 19. Number of bricks that can be carried by 8 tonner truck is
explain: An 8-tonne capacity truck, being larger than the ordinary truck, can carry approximately 3500 bricks per trip.

q: 20. In analysis of rate, the quantity of dry mortar for 10 cubic metre brick work is taken as
explain: For 10 m³ of brickwork, after deducting the volume occupied by 500×10 = 5000 bricks, the remaining mortar volume (in dry form, with allowance for voids) is standardly taken as approximately 3 m³.

q: 21. One cubic metre of cement concrete (1 : 2 : 4) is to be mixed by volume. Number of cement bags required will be approximately
explain: For 1 m³ of 1:2:4 concrete, dry volume ≈ 1.54 m³, cement fraction = 1/7, giving cement volume ≈ 0.22 m³; dividing by 0.035 m³ per bag gives approximately 6 bags.

q: 22. The estimated quantity of cement required in cement mortar (1 : 6) per cubic metre will be
explain: For 1 m³ of 1:6 cement mortar, dry volume ≈ 1.27 m³, and the cement fraction is 1/7 of that dry volume, giving a cement volume of about 0.18 m³; dividing by 0.035 m³ per bag gives approximately 5.6 bags.

q: 23. Thickness of plastering is usually
explain: The standard thickness adopted for ordinary wall plastering is 12 mm, unless a special finish requires otherwise.

q: 24. One cubic metre of mild steel weights about
explain: As established earlier, the density of mild steel is approximately 7850 kg/m³, giving this same weight for one cubic metre.

q: 25. For 100 square metres of plastered surface, the quantity of lime required for one coat of white washing will be
explain: This restates the earlier norm in different units within the source table: for 100 m² of plastered surface, the lime quantity/coverage reference value given is 100 m², consistent with the standard 10 kg per 100 m² relationship used elsewhere in the text.

q: 26. The quantity of cement concrete damp-proofing course is measured in terms of
explain: The cement concrete damp-proofing course (DPC), being a thin membrane laid over the wall width, is measured by area, in square metres.
